newsitem.title: CHINA: China open market operations small, but to expand.
newsitem.headline: China open market operations small, but to expand.

text.p: China's long-awaited expansion of central open market operations, announced on Friday, will probably make the market more than symbolic, but volumes are still expected to be very light, analysts said on Monday.
"The expansion will change the nature of the operations," said a banker with a major Chinese state bank. "In the first year, the operations were nothing but symbolic."

China launched the open operations in April 1996 to provide a mechanism for adjusting money supply and to give the markets a clearer indication of monetary policy, but only a small four billion yuan ($482 million) has been traded so far.

On Friday, Beijing announced it would expand the number of institutions participating in the operations to 25 from 14, and the central bank announced it planned new issues of short-term treasury bills to facilitate the operations.

"With more banks participating in the operations, the central bank can more effectively give an indication of its thinking on monetary policy," an official with the central bank's open market operations section told Reuters.
A foreign banker in Shanghai said the expansion of open operations was a good sign, but that the market was still obviously viewed by the central bank as an experiment.

"It's an improvement but quite minor," the banker said. "The bottom line is that it's still experimental, and they don't have the means to go the full way, to really make it a market which would regulate interest rates as it would in the West."
Chinese bankers said the new move was unlikely in the short-term to help the central bank make the operations an effective means of manipulating money supply.

"The operations will not be able to be useful in adjusting money supply in the foreseeable future due to a lack of tradable short-term debt and the exclusion of major non-bank financial institutions," one banker said.
The names of the new banks to be included have not been announced, but a central bank official said they would include major city cooperative banks in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing.
"The central bank is pushing the cooperative banks to increase their role, to be more competitive and to put pressure on the state banks," the foreign banker said.
Chinese bankers said open operations stopped at the end of last year to allow central bank officials to re-think the strategy for expanding the market.

But they said that with the expansion of the number of market participants and the issue last Friday of a new set of rules governing the operations, the market was set for an early resumption of trading.

No securities houses or trust and investment firms are included in the operations at this point, but are expected to be included eventually, the bankers said. They declined to speculate on a timetable.

"On the whole, they are sensible to use this cautious approach," the foreign banker said. "I can understand it, they feel the market is immature, the players are immature, and they don't want to have any big ups and downs in the market." ($1=8.3 yuan)
